sources.source: Art. 17 GDPR: Right to erasure (GDPR text)

items.item: the data subject shall have the right to obtain from the controller the erasure of personal data concerning him or her without undue delay

at.step: Reveal: erasure against both designs, measured

sources.source: Art. 5 GDPR: Principles relating to processing (GDPR text)

items.item: personal data must be kept in a form which permits identification of data subjects for no longer than is necessary for the purposes for which the personal data are processed

at.step: Reveal: what keeping raw forever costs

items.item: A correction to a raw record arrives as a brand-new, later-offset record, never as an edit to the record it corrects, measured directly: the first three records in the raw layer stay byte-for-byte unmutated after a fourth, correcting record is appended.

at.step: Reveal: raw capture is append-only, measured

items.item: A raw record's three metadata fields (ingest time, source offset, schema version) are what make a replay trustworthy rather than a guess; stripping any one out removes the information a rebuild needs to know exactly what arrived, when, and under which assumptions.

at.step: Reveal: the three metadata fields

items.item: Two builds of a silver table from the identical raw layer and the identical transform land on byte-identical checksums, measured directly, proving the raw layer alone decides silver's contents regardless of what happened to any prior silver table.

at.step: Reveal: rebuild by replay, measured

items.item: Rebuilding with a fixed transform changes only the rows the original bug actually touched, measured directly: of four orders, only the two in a foreign currency differ between the buggy and fixed builds, while the two already in the right currency land identical in both.

at.step: Reveal: a bug fix isolated by replay, measured

items.item: Keeping raw data forever for replayability directly works against the storage-limitation duty to keep personal data no longer than necessary — this topic names the tension rather than claiming a universal resolution, and shows one concrete mitigation for the one field that actually identifies a person.

at.step: Reveal: what keeping raw forever costs

items.item: Tokenizing the one identifying field makes a small, separate vault the only mutable part of an otherwise append-only design, and satisfying an erasure request against it requires deleting exactly one vault row, measured directly against a plaintext raw layer's own requirement to mutate three historical records for the identical request.

at.step: Reveal: erasure against both designs, measured

items.item: The wrong half of the predict question — that fixing historical numbers requires a fresh extraction from the live source — is ruled out directly: the bug lived entirely in the transform, and the raw layer's own unprocessed records were never affected by it, so a replay with the fixed transform alone reaches the correct result.

at.step: Predict: fixing without re-extracting

items.item: The wrong half of the final predict question — blanking out a token in every raw record naming the erased person — reintroduces the plaintext design's own failure by hand; the whole purpose of tokenization is that the raw layer never needs to be touched for an erasure, only the vault's one mapping does.

at.step: Prove it

items.item: This topic hosts no lab of its own, per CHAPTER.md's own table — the rebuild-by-replay check and the bug-fix-isolation check are this topic's own measured examples, not a shared lab leg.

at.out: no lab of its own, per CHAPTER.md

items.item: Chapter 3 topic 19's medallion architecture and its own failure modes are the layering structure this topic's raw layer sits inside, used and not re-derived; GDPR's erasure mechanics in full and Chapter 13's own treatment of them are named and left untaught here.
